html:
Aboriginal Australians are the Indigenous peoples of mainland Australia and most of its islands. Their ancestors arrived from Southeast Asia 50,000 to 65,000 years ago, so their societies run back far beyond the start of this chart and are among the oldest continuous cultures on earth.

Over that time they formed several hundred nations, each tied to its own territory, or "Country", with its own language and law. At the time of British settlement more than 250 languages were spoken. People lived through the Ice Age, when Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania were joined by land, and through the rise of the sea that later cut them apart.

Wall charts usually leave them out because there are no dynasties or capitals to draw. What they built instead:

  • Detailed knowledge of land, water and seasons, passed on through song, story and ceremony, often called the Dreaming.
  • Fire-stick burning that shaped whole landscapes, eel traps and fish traps, and long trade routes for ochre, stone and shells.
  • Rock art among the oldest in the world.
  • Contacts beyond the continent, with Torres Strait Islanders and with fishermen from Sulawesi in the Makassan trepang trade.

The arrival of the First Fleet in 1788 began colonisation by Britain. Smallpox, frontier killings and the loss of land cut the population sharply. In the 20th century governments took children from their families, the Stolen Generations. The Mabo case of 1992 overturned the claim that Australia had been empty land, and painting movements such as Papunya Tula brought Aboriginal art to the world.
